extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers of science, and students of scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative standards for inductive investigation: how to infer causes from observed phenomena, the limits of purely observational/experimental methods, and how to state and test laws in the presence of multiple or interacting causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Infer a possible common cause by comparing instances that share the same antecedent(s) and the same consequent(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Method of Agreement yields only suggestions when the number of instances is small because the same effect may have different causes in different instances. It becomes valuable only when instances are numerous and sufficiently varied so that the possibility of a plurality of causes is rebutted. Even then, conclusions from this method should be confirmed by the Method of Difference or by deductive connection with already ascertained laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare a positive instance (with A present producing a) and a negative instance (without A producing not-a) — if adding A converts the negative into the positive, A is the cause (or an indispensable part of the cause) of a in that case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Method of Difference is rigorous and not vitiated by the Plurality of Causes: two instances (one positive, one negative) suffice for a complete induction regarding that instance. Use it to test and establish causal claims suggested by the Method of Agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Method of Agreement and Difference (Indirect Method of Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine agreement and difference: instances in which the phenomenon is present agree only in containing A, and instances in which it is absent agree only in not containing A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method ensures A is the only possible cause and thus is immensely more powerful than simple Agreement. It is especially valuable in sciences depending mainly on observation and is often the primary resource where direct experiments are hard to perform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four Methods as methods of proof for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The four empirical methods (Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations, and Joint methods) constitute the sole methods of proof for inductive claims; even results of deduction must ultimately be amenable to them for empirical validation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when hypotheses arise by deduction, they must end by being proved by these methods. Induction requires tests analogous to syllogistic tests of deduction; absence of such proof is a serious weakness in a proposed induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurality of Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The same phenomenon may be produced by several independent causes or assemblages of conditions; an effect may sometimes arise from A, sometimes from B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plurality of Causes undermines the reliability of the Method of Agreement unless a wide and varied set of instances can be shown to exclude other antecedents. The practical effect is that mere repetition of similar instances adds little evidence; varying circumstances and appeals to probability theory are needed to know when the plurality hypothesis is rebutted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermixture of Effects / Composition of Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple causes act together their separate effects may be compounded, cancelled, or merged so that the observable result does not plainly display the individual contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition of Causes often eludes direct inductive methods; deduction is usually required to unravel the contributing causes. Recognize cases where effects are +a, -a, 1/2 b, etc., and be cautious about inferring simple relations from complex, compounded results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heteropathic effects and transformation (chemical composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: When causes combine to produce a qualitatively new phenomenon (heteropathic effect or transformation), this new phenomenon has its own laws and can often be subjected to experimental inquiry; analysis of the new effect may reveal its producing agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such cases are more amenable to experiment (e.g., water from hydrogen and oxygen). Chemical analysis searches for causes among the effects of the compound; sometimes the compound under some conditions reproduces its agents, aiding discovery (Lavoisier examples). But many heteropathic cases (e.g., complex mental states) cannot be decomposed by reversing the process and require synthetic study of simple constituents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of negative instances in induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the Method of Agreement to negative instances (cases where the phenomenon does not occur) is free from the characteristic imperfection that affects affirmative Agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative-instance Agreement can be powerful because showing what negatives have in common can indicate the absence of a cause. In practice it is often infeasible because exhausting or cataloguing the field of negation is very difficult; therefore investigators usually study positives first and then test absence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressing laws as tendencies rather than absolute results
rubrics_metrics.description: Because causes can be counteracted by other causes, general causal laws should be stated as tendencies (e.g., 'tends to move') not as absolute inevitabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use terminology that records tendencies (e.g., 'pressure' as tendency to motion) or qualifiers like 'unless prevented' or 'except in so far as prevented.' This avoids the misleading popular impression that scientific laws admit arbitrary exceptions and correctly represents concurrent principles acting together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of the number of instances
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere mass or number of observed instances has value only insofar as it helps to exclude the hypothesis of Plurality of Causes by showing the same antecedent across varied circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeating identical-type instances without varying circumstances adds no new evidence. A single instance that rules out an antecedent common to other cases can be more valuable than many redundant ones. When possible, vary conditions and attempt to eliminate antecedents rather than relying on quantity alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting plurality when it actually exists
rubrics_metrics.description: When an effect is genuinely producible by multiple distinct causes, detection follows the same processes as for single causes: separate sequences of instances may reveal different causes, or collating instances may show no single antecedent present in all cases but that one or another of several is always present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no common antecedent is found but one or other of several antecedents always occurs, set these antecedents down provisionally as distinct sufficient causes. Further analysis may reveal a deeper common element; if not, treat them as separate causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating concurrent causes as additive for prediction/explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of predicting, calculating, or explaining joint results, causes that compound may be treated as if each produced its own effect and the net result is their sum (e.g., forces producing diagonal motion or equilibrium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This viewpoint clarifies that laws are fulfilled even when counteracted: each cause 'tends' to produce its effect and does so fully in the sense that its energy would have produced an equivalent result absent opposing causes. Use this conception to avoid categorical contradictions when stating general laws.
